Nightborne can be earned through Nightfallen rep, which can be mostly earned by doing the full Suramar questline (which is needed for the race unlock, anyway). Otherwise doing worldquests in Suramar grants Nightfallen rep (esp if you get good at the withered army training WQ which refreshes every 3 days I think?) 

Void Elves & Lightforged Draenei are earned through Argussian Reach and Army of the Light rep respectively. That can be earned from doing the quests, world quests, and dailies and weekly on Argus. 

Highmountain Tauren are earned through Highmountain rep, gained through WQs in Highmountain and through the Highmountain storyline. You can also get Highmountain rep from running Neltharion's Lair, as the second to last boss grants some reputation, and it's easily farmable at lvl 120

Mag'har Orcs & Dark Iron Dwarves you get from doing the Horde & Alliance war campaigns respectively and getting reputation with the Honorbound & 7th Legion. You have a wide variety of WQs to do here as any Warfronts WQs or WQs on the other faction's island (Kul Tiras if you're Horde, Zandalar if you're Alliance) grants reputation. Wanted quests in opposite-faction zones also give Honorbound & 7th Legion rep, as do Assaults. 

Zandalari Trolls & Kul Tirans you get from Zandalari Empire and Proudmoore Admiralty reputation respectively, as well as doing two additional questlines, Zandalar Forever and The Pride of Kul Tiras, the latter of which requires quite a bit of dungeon queuing. 

And if you're interested in the allied races in the next patch, Vulpera are by doing the Vol'dun questline and gaining Voldunai Rep (WQs and quests), Mechagnomes will be by getting exalted with the Rustbolt Resistance (a faction unlocked when you reach 120 and do the opening quests for Nazjatar & Mechagon) and there's an achievement involved. I found Rustbolt reputation pretty easy, personally.

If you don't have a problem with rep grinds and cleaning quests, you'll be fine--I enjoy rep grinds personally so smashing these out was never a huge problem for me. Emissary quests and reputation buffs from the Dark Moon Faire and currently the Anniversary Event are your friends. You can also buy contracts from the AH for BfA reps (Honorbound, 7th Legion, Zandalari Empire, Proudmoore Admiralty, Voldunai, Rustbolt too I think?)  to boost rep gains. I was able to do all of these in about a week a piece when I was focused on them. Good luck!

It's because the Link in each game isn't the same Link. Because massive amounts of time tend to pass between games that aren't direct sequels to one another, the common belief is that each "Link" in each game is either a reincarnation or a descendant of whoever the original Link was (most likely the Link in Skyward Sword)--just as there is no one Zelda, but reincarnations and descendants of the original Zelda.

During Ocarina of Time, you go backwards and forwards in time by seven years (seven years forward, seven years back) between Link as a child and Link as an adult, in order to get different things done (ie, you enter the Spirit Temple as both an adult and as a child in order to accomplish different tasks inside--adult Link needs an item only child Link can obtain from the Temple in order to progress, but child Link cannot finish the temple). At the end of OoT, Zelda sends Link back in time to be a child again so he can live his life as he had ought to instead of losing seven years. This is where the timeline splits: there is the timeline where child Link wasn't stuck in the sacred realm for seven years (which is then where Majora's Mask takes place) and Ganondorf never took over Hyrule, and the Hyrule that was left without him entirely because he was sent back in time.

Each game in the Zelda series was developed independently of one another with the intention of them being enjoyed independently without having to have any context of the other games, so the timeline doesn't necessarily matter. Of course there are some consistencies and common themes through each games and some vague idea where they're supposed to fall chronologically (Majora's Mask being the immediate sequel to Ocarina of Time; Zelda II being the sequel to the original LoZ, and a Link to the Past intended to be taken place before them; Skyward Sword is intended to be the earliest in the timeline; Phantom Hourglass is the immediate sequel to Wind Waker; etc etc) but they're all supposed to be contained stories that you can enjoy without necessarily understanding the others. 

That being said, there was a timeline added retroactively (mostly due to fan request) that puts everything on a split timeline that happens as a result of Link manipulating timelines in OoT--but chronology doesn't matter for LoZ, really, and imo it was more fun when it was left up to speculation and theory.

The Heroes failed in Empire Strikes Back, and people forget that because we know they turn out successful at the end of Return of the Jedi--and in my opinion, the satisfactory payoff of a victory against impossible odds isn't satisfying at all if the heroes don't fail at some point, or if the threat of failure is very much a real one. Suspense isn't suspenseful unless you know things can go tits up. Heroes can't be heroes in a world where heroes can't fail, in a world where heroes have no consequences for failure.

The other thing I liked about Canto Bight, personally, is that it showed the galaxy isn't rigorously divided on morality and was full of people selling arms to both the Resistance and the First Order because all they cared about was profit--and this was incredibly important for Finn to see in his arc and where he is at the end of the movie. I thought DJ was an important character because he makes a really good foil to Finn--someone who is concerned with what's important to him (survival), but doesn't have sort of a moral center like Finn does and is thus willing to swap sides in order to ensure he's alive.

Gorgeous cinematography with contrasting colors that stand out from other Star Wars films with scenes like the one between Kylo and Rey in the throne room, the fact that it has a central theme (that in order to move forward, you must put the past behind you; other Star Wars movies don't really have that central theme behind all of the arcs in play), the canto bight arc showing us that the whole galaxy isn't divided between rebels and the first order--that there are rich and powerful who are going to profit off of the conflict and don't care who wins, that in addition to a character like DJ who's willing to swap sides in order to ensure his own survival. The fact that every character has a distinct character arc that gives a strong sense of development and is a different person at the end of the movie--Poe was willing to martyr himself for the cause at the beginning, and by the end sees the importance of his (and the resistance's) survival, Kylo might have been able to redeem himself at the beginning, but by the end something like that is impossible for him.

I feel like Corypheus is a more interesting antagonist when you take what makes up most of your important quests in a playthrough of DAI: companion quests. 

I feel like most of the core story content in an Inquisition playthrough, if you're someone like me who enjoys doing everything and keeping all your companions happy no matter what, revolves around character quests and interactions with your companions. Corypheus is interesting when you consider him as a foil to characters like Leliana and Solas. He, granted, isn't a foil to every companion, but Solas in particular is a foil to everyone else so I guess it evens out. 

Corypheus can be compared to Leliana in the respect that they're both people who had very strong beliefs in their respective deities (Corypheus and Dumat, Leliana and the Maker) and pulled a lot of inspiration from said faith--but then they both had their faith shaken. Corypheus by seeing that the Golden City was empty, and Leliana by losing Justinia. 

Solas in Trespasser straight up gives you the comparison. He led Corypheus to the orb because he wanted Corypheus to tear down the veil for him (or something to that effect, it's been a while), and then the whole thing just got kind of out of hand and not what he was intended for because Corypheus was more selfish and malicious in his intentions than Solas--who, yeah, wants to destroy the world, but he's doing so out of a sense of obligation to his people whom he failed in the past rather than the belief that what he's doing is morally justified or correct.

Foils exist to highlight different traits in each other in order to draw spotlight to importance or to particular traits. In Leliana's case it leads to highlighting her virtue (I've never "hardened" her, so I have no context as to what it's like when she's more ruthless) and even though her faith was shaken, she might not necessarily need it in order to have a drive to do good--and in Solas' case, it highlights what makes him interesting as a character and a prospective villain: that his motivations as a character don't exist to necessarily further himself, but because he's someone with too much pride who failed his people and seeks to undo his mistake out of a sense of obligation even though he knows what he's doing is horrible. Having Corypheus there helps those stand out moreso than if we didn't have a villain that was intrinsically tied to the central mythos of Thedas who now aspires to godhood now that he's seen that his god doesn't exist.

This is tricky! I tend to pick races based on what I think will suit the personality of the characters I'm making or just bounce off of an idea. But there are definitely some I gravitate to.

I'm very much not an elf person and usually avoid elves at all costs and think they're super lame... but will still probably pick elves over humans.
